topology: Three user-approved Ubuntu VMs with distinct kernels on one physical host; six real Redis 8.2 nodes (three primaries, three cross-VM replicas); IAM/Gateway on manager, Auth/BFF on each worker; isolated MySQL/proxies/browser on host.

run.environment: Three independent Ubuntu VMs; real 3-primary/3-replica Redis Cluster; real IAM, Gateway, 2 Auth, 2 BFF

cases.name: synchronized Redis Cluster automatic failover after lost commit reply
replication-lag failover after acknowledged organization commit
replication-lag failover after acknowledged logout and RT revocation
original absolute deadline with clustered session and RT after topology changes

regressionExecutionThisRound: No Java/frontend production source changes. The prior 288-test result is reference evidence, not rerun or a substitute for this failed distributed acceptance.
rootCause: All authoritative BFF binding/session/transaction data, Auth operation idempotency, authorization and online/revocation state can roll back with asynchronous Redis replication. Revalidation consults the available but reverted state; single-node CAS/hash tags do not provide an external irreversible revocation/issuance fence.
methodology: Only newly labeled containers/directories/ports were modified. Existing demo services were not stopped or deleted.

Application partition used actual kernel OUTPUT drops to the owned Redis endpoints; replication lag used INPUT drops in only the new replica container namespaces, leaving cluster voting traffic available.
Healthy baseline used SET plus WAIT on the same connection for each primary. Lagged writes occurred afterwards while replica data traffic was blocked.
Primary processes were killed in sequence; replicas promoted through automatic elections. No CLUSTER FAILOVER FORCE/TAKEOVER or injected business responses were used.

FLUSHALL was used only on the new exclusive cluster before the real application environment started, to discard failed startup artifacts. No keys were manually restored/edited to create the observed rollback.
Normal API calls and replay checks used actual server credentials, CSRF, precise Origin, device fingerprint and current-context proof; credentials never entered this report.
limitations: Independent virtual hosts share a physical computer; physical power failure and separate datacenters are outside this run.
Data directories used owned tmpfs in each VM; this verifies replication/election rollback rather than physical disk durability.
Self-signed HTTPS trust was bypassed in isolated Chrome.

Observed VM clock offset estimates were approximately +0.7 to +0.9 seconds relative to the host, with recorded RTT uncertainty; all VMs reported synchronized NTP. Natural expiry was checked after the declared cutoff plus 1.5 seconds.

Client revalidation and current-token checks cannot distinguish valid current state from an authoritative store restored to an earlier valid state. Fixing this requires a reviewed consistency design; no production code or deployed environment was changed this round.
